tldr: To eliminate the inference latency of large language models during robot control, this paper proposes a framework that bakes trial-and-error experience into executable Python programs, achieving autonomous, high-success-rate (92.1%) real-world manipulation.
hero_caption: Overview of ACE-CaP-0. A coding agent iteratively refines code using robot demonstrations and simulation as needed, then "freezes" the finished program to run autonomously on physical hardware. It achieves an overall success rate of 92.1% across eight real-world tasks.
overview:
Recently, using frontier models (high-capability LLMs) as robotic agents to perform tasks through trial and error has attracted major interest. However, invoking a massive model at every execution step leads to substantial inference latency, creating a fundamental bottleneck where task completion times balloon significantly.

To address this, Code as Policies (CaP) has gained traction. CaP represents robot control policies directly as executable programs. By capturing the reasoning invested during the trial-and-error development phase into executable code like Python, the robot can run at execution time using fast runtime perception and control, completely bypassing the LLM. Nevertheless, physical trial and error carries heavy costs, including human scene resets and robot wear-and-tear. Developing reliable code within a realistic experimentation budget remains a critical challenge.

The authors first conducted an in-depth investigation on a "charger insertion" task, exploring different human guidance modalities (text, human video, robot demonstrations), timing (upfront vs. on-request), and simulation usage patterns. They found that pairing "Demonstrations on Request"—called only when the agent gets stuck—with "Simulation on Demand"—used selectively to verify specific subproblems—yields the best results.

These findings led to the development recipe called "ACE-CaP-0." Under a strict budget of at most 10 real-world scene resets per task, they applied the recipe to eight real-world manipulation tasks involving bimanual coordination and precision alignment. The resulting frozen programs achieved an impressive 92.1% overall success rate across 240 trials (221/240).
contributions: Established ACE-CaP-0, a policy development recipe that minimizes physical trial-and-error costs (such as human scene resets) while producing reliable code policies.

Demonstrated that providing robot demonstrations "On-Request" when the agent identifies a need is far superior in both development efficiency and final task performance compared to providing comprehensive upfront guidance.

Revealed that "Simulation on Demand"—invoking simulation locally from within the real-world development loop to verify specific hypotheses—avoids the observation gap and works far better than sequential Sim-to-Real exploration.

Showed that frozen programs running without an LLM or human in the loop achieve an overall success rate of 92.1% with mean execution times ranging from 0.97 to 2.27 minutes across eight real-world tasks, including bimanual coordination and precision insertion.

sections.heading: Breaking the Latency Barrier: Turning Experience into Programs
sections.summary: Repeatedly calling an LLM inside the robot control loop causes severe inference latency. This highlights the importance of CaP, which preserves trial-and-error experience as executable code. We explore how to best utilize demonstrations and simulation while keeping physical trial costs low.
sections.details:
Recent advances in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and frontier models have enabled robots to autonomously perceive their surroundings and act. However, querying a massive model at every single step accumulates significant communication and computation latency, causing tasks to take an excessively long time to complete.

To solve this, this work focuses on Code as Policies (CaP). In CaP, the robot's control policy is output as program code containing action sequences, geometric computations, and trajectory parameters. When a coding agent (an LLM) spends the effort reasoning and experimenting during development, it bakes that reasoning into code. At runtime, the agent can be removed from the loop, allowing the robot to execute standalone with high speed.

However, developing reliable code policies from scratch is difficult. A prompt alone cannot specify the countless physical preconditions needed, such as grasp strategies or approach trajectories. When an execution fails on physical hardware, it is not immediately obvious which part of the code needs fixing. Moreover, physical experiments require a human to perform tedious, time-consuming scene resets.

Therefore, policy revision must be smartly coupled with physical experience acquisition. This paper investigates how to best combine human guidance and simulation to develop robust programs with minimal physical trials.

sections.heading: In-Depth Investigation: How Should We Use Guidance and Simulation?
sections.summary: Using a charger insertion task, we compared guidance modalities, timing, and simulation strategies. The results revealed that "Demonstrations on Request" and "Simulation on Demand"—calling the simulator locally from the real-world loop—are the most effective.
sections.details:
The authors tested six experimental conditions on a challenging "charger insertion" task (plugging a charger into a power strip) to evaluate different ways of incorporating human guidance and simulation. For a fair comparison, all conditions strictly capped human scene resets at a maximum of 10 interventions.

### 2.1 How Should Human Priors Be Incorporated?
First, they compared three guidance modalities:
- Text-only advice
- Robot-Egocentric Human Video
- Robot Demonstrations (direct kinesthetic teaching, providing joint trajectories and key poses in addition to video)

Robot Demonstrations achieved the highest success rate at 86.7% (26/30 trials), significantly outperforming human video (73.3%) and text-only guidance (60.0%). While human videos require translating human hand motions into robot arm joint angles, robot demonstrations directly provide arm configurations and trajectory numerical data, making it much easier for the agent to incorporate them into code.

Next, they compared guidance timing. They tested "Upfront" guidance (all provided at the beginning) against "On-Request" guidance (provided when the agent requested it). The difference was stark. Upfront guidance resulted in a 53.3% success rate and took 7.2 hours of development time. In contrast, On-Request guidance achieved an 86.7% success rate in just 3.7 hours—nearly cutting development time in half while substantially boosting performance. Providing too much information upfront causes cognitive overload for the agent, whereas targeted guidance at the exact point of failure drastically improves revision accuracy.

### 2.2 How Should Simulation Be Incorporated?
Next, they evaluated three simulation strategies:
- Real-Only (developing purely on real hardware)
- Sequential Real-Sim-Real (building a simulator, exploring 10 rounds in parallel, then transferring to the real robot)
- Simulation on Demand (invoking simulation only when questions arise during real-world development)

Surprisingly, the conventional Sequential Real-Sim-Real pipeline yielded a 0% real-world success rate. The agent overfitted to clean simulation depth images and failed to handle the near-field blind spots and sensor noise of the real LiDAR and depth cameras, failing at the initial plug grasp. Conversely, Simulation on Demand, which keeps physical execution primary and uses simulation only to compare candidate policies, achieved a 100% success rate and reduced development time to 2.6 hours. It proves extremely powerful because it enables safe verification without breaking real-world sensing assumptions.

sections.heading: The Policy Recipe: Autonomously Gathering Experience to Refine Code
sections.summary: Synthesizing our investigation findings, we define the ACE-CaP-0 recipe. The coding agent autonomously chooses between real-world trials, on-request demonstrations, and on-demand simulation to refine code, eventually freezing it into a standalone executable program.
sections.details:
Based on the findings in Section 2, the authors formulated the ACE-CaP-0 policy development recipe. This recipe consists of two phases: a policy development phase and a standalone execution phase.

### 3.1 Integrated Policy Development Loop
The agent takes the task instruction and workspace observations to write initial code. Its toolbox includes perception and control interfaces for the robot. Inside the development loop, it iterates through "write code -> execute on robot -> inspect results -> revise code," with the flexibility to choose its next action:
- Execute on the real robot to inspect physical behavior
- Request a human robot demonstration when completely unsure of the strategy (Demonstrations on Request)
- Spin up a simulator to test multiple approach trajectories or collision behaviors (Simulation on Demand)

### 3.2 Demonstrations on Request
The agent requests demonstrations only when it determines that it does not know how to proceed. Through direct kinesthetic teaching—where a human physically moves the robot arm—the system records not only camera feeds but also joint angle trajectories and key poses at critical moments. From these trajectories, the agent extracts geometric and kinematic constraints (such as where to grasp a bag or how to perform a bimanual handover) and encodes them into program variables and function calls.

### 3.3 Simulation on Demand
The agent initializes the simulator specifically for sub-tasks where uncertainties arise. For instance, to evaluate which approach trajectory avoids collisions, it isolates the specific step and initial state, testing candidate programs in parallel. Once it identifies a promising candidate in simulation, it immediately brings it back to the real robot for validation. This prevents the agent from overfitting to simulation-specific visual representations.

### 3.4 Standalone Execution with Frozen Programs
Once development is complete, the final code is "frozen." During standalone evaluation, neither the coding agent nor a human is in the loop. The frozen program computes object poses in real time from live camera images and depth sensors, commanding the arms via APIs. This completely eliminates model inference latency, achieving fast and deterministic control.

captions.F5: System architecture of ACE-CaP-0. (a) During development, the agent requests real demonstrations or performs simulation experiments as needed, revising code through the physical loop. (b) The finalized code policy is frozen and runs standalone during evaluation without agent or human intervention.

sections.heading: Real-World Evaluation: 92.1% Success Across Diverse Bimanual Tasks
sections.summary: We evaluated eight challenging manipulation tasks on a dual-arm, three-camera robot platform. Across 30 trials per task (240 trials total), the frozen programs achieved an overall success rate of 92.1% with mean execution times ranging from 0.97 to 2.27 minutes.
sections.details:
To evaluate the generality of the proposed recipe, the authors conducted extensive real-world experiments across eight diverse manipulation tasks.

### 4.1 Evaluation Setup
The experimental setup featured two Agilex PIPERX robot arms and three Orbbec DaBai DC1 cameras (one top-down overhead view and two wrist-mounted cameras). Claude Opus 5.5 served as the base model for the coding agent. During development, real-world scene resets were strictly limited to a maximum of 10 resets per task (excluding resets used for gathering demonstrations). Once development finished, the generated code was frozen and evaluated across 30 real-world trials per task with randomized initial configurations, totaling 240 trials.

### 4.2 Task Performance and Details
The results demonstrated high reliability, achieving an overall success rate of 92.1% (221/240 trials). Seven of the eight tasks achieved success rates of 90% or higher:
- **Charger Insertion**: 30/30 (100%), mean execution time 1.65 min. Successfully executed high-precision alignment into a narrow socket.
- **Chicken Plating**: 29/30 (96.7%), mean 1.12 min. Detected irregularly shaped items and arranged them on a plate.
- **Cup Nesting**: 28/30 (93.3%), mean 1.58 min.
- **Parcel Reorientation**: 28/30 (93.3%), mean 0.97 min. Completed in under a minute, the fastest among all tasks.
- **Flower Insertion**: 27/30 (90.0%), mean 1.37 min.
- **Bottle Uncapping**: 27/30 (90.0%), mean 2.23 min. Coordinated bimanual manipulation: one arm stabilized the bottle while the other untwisted the cap.
- **Shoe Packing**: 27/30 (90.0%), mean 2.27 min. Coordinated both arms to pack a pair of shoes into a box.
- **Bread Packing**: 25/30 (83.3%), mean 1.93 min. Maintained a high success rate despite struggling with grasping deformable plastic packaging.

Execution speed was particularly notable. Six out of eight tasks took less than two minutes on average, with the longest task averaging 2.27 minutes. Because agentic control calling an LLM at every step can easily take anywhere from several minutes to tens of minutes, freezing policies as executable programs proves highly practical.

sections.heading: Related Work: Weaving Physical Experience into Autonomous Improvement
sections.summary: We review prior work across Code-as-Policies, agentic self-improvement, and the use of demonstrations and simulation. ACE-CaP-0 distinguishes itself by integrating on-request demonstrations and on-demand simulation within a constrained real-world budget.
sections.details:
This work sits at the intersection of code generation for robot control and experiential learning in the physical world.

### Code-Based Robot Control and Self-Improving Agents
Alongside end-to-end models like VLAs, Code-as-Policies (CaP) approaches have gained significant traction. Programmatic representations offer the clear advantage that their logical structures and geometric parameters can be directly inspected and modified by humans and LLMs. Furthermore, agents using Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) to iteratively revise code by analyzing execution logs have emerged, but most remain confined to simulation. The primary obstacles to running self-improvement loops on real hardware are human reset burdens and limited trial budgets.

### Positioning Guidance and Simulation
While many imitation learning studies use human demonstrations, this work focuses on an interactive framework where the agent actively requests demonstrations ("On-Request") the moment it encounters uncertainty. Additionally, while Sim-to-Real gaps are a perennial issue in simulation research, this study proposes a new paradigm: using the simulator not upfront ("Sequential"), but "on demand" as a targeted hypothesis-testing tool within the real-world development loop. This successfully avoids the observation gap trap, enabling safe and rapid code refinement.

sections.heading: Conclusion and Next Steps: Transforming Experience into Reusable Skills
sections.summary: ACE-CaP-0 combines demonstrations on request and simulation on demand to deliver highly reliable (92.1%) code policies while limiting physical experimentation costs. Future work includes policy reuse in new environments and automated trade-off estimation for experience acquisition.
sections.details:
ACE-CaP-0 demonstrates an effective recipe for turning agentic trial-and-error experience into deterministic programs that run autonomously at runtime. The core takeaways—calling demonstrations on request and using simulation on demand within the physical loop—provide practical guidelines for preventing policy divergence while minimizing physical scene resets.

### Limitations and Future Work
The authors note that their detailed comparative investigations relied on a single task (charger insertion) across single development runs. Future work should verify reproducibility across multiple independent development runs and evaluate policy reuse across diverse tasks.

Additionally, building algorithms that allow the agent to estimate the value of acquiring additional experience (human demonstrations or simulation) beforehand—balancing it against human time, LLM token costs, and robot run time—represents an important next research direction.

takeaways: To eliminate LLM inference latency, baking trial-and-error experience into deterministic Python programs during development and "freezing" them for runtime execution is highly effective.

Rather than providing all human demonstrations upfront, offering them "On-Request" when the agent encounters uncertainty or failure cuts development time in half and dramatically improves success rates.

To avoid the Sim-to-Real observation gap, simulation should not be used as a standalone prerequisite; instead, it should be called on demand from within the real-world loop to test targeted hypotheses.
limitations: Detailed comparative investigations on guidance modalities and simulation strategies were conducted on a single development run of a single task (charger insertion).
Human demonstration effort and setup time were not factored into the quantitative cost accounting (token usage and scene reset budgets).
Success rates remained in the 80% range for tasks involving complex contact mechanics and deformable objects, such as grasping a flexible bread bag.
